vignette:
He tells the story like a report at first—flat, professional, as if he’s giving a briefing to a new supervisor. But his hands give him away. They rest on his knees, gripping the fabric of his uniform trousers, then releasing, then gripping again. Raj is forty-one, a park ranger in a large forest reserve in southern India, and for fourteen years he knew every trail, every waterhole, every sound the jungle made after dark. That knowledge is what saved him, and that knowledge is what haunts him now.

It happened during the dry season, four years ago. He was on a routine patrol in a section of the reserve that bordered a logging road, an area he had warned his team about for months. He remembers the heat, the smell of dust and dry leaves, the way the cicadas went quiet just before the truck appeared. Three men, one with a rifle. They grabbed him from behind, pinned his arms, and shoved a burlap sack over his head. He still feels the coarse fabric scraping his lips when he tries to describe it, and he stops, swallows, then continues.

They kept him for eleven days in a makeshift camp deep in the forest. His own forest. He could hear the calls of langurs and peacocks, familiar sounds turned strange. They questioned him about patrol schedules, ranger checkpoints, the location of camera traps. He gave them nothing, but that didn’t seem to matter. They tied him to a tree at night, wrists raw from the rope. They fed him once a day—cold rice, sometimes with a piece of dried fish. He learned to count the hours by the movement of shadows on the ground where he sat, his back against the bark, his ankles bound. He learned to tell when a man was about to strike by the way his shadow leaned forward, the line of his arm rising. That knowledge sits in his body now, a muscle memory he cannot turn off.

After eleven days, a patrol found the camp during a sweep. There was a brief exchange of fire. Raj was left behind as the men fled. He remembers the sound of boots on dry leaves, running away, and then silence. He stayed sitting against the tree even after the rangers called his name. He could not move his legs. He thought they were still tied.

In the months that followed, he returned to work. The park service gave him a desk job—paperwork, permit reviews, scheduling. He accepted it without complaint. He told himself he was fine. But the forest began to feel different. He could no longer walk a trail without his heart accelerating at every snapped twig. He stopped eating fish because the texture reminded him of the cold rice. He began to scan the treeline constantly, even when he was in his own backyard. His partner, Anjali, noticed he no longer wanted to sit outside at night. He made excuses—mosquitoes, the cold—but really it was the darkness. The darkness had become a thing that could hold him.

He started carrying a knife in his pocket, even to the grocery store. He checks the locks on their apartment door three times before bed. The sound of a car door slamming on the street makes him freeze mid-sentence, and he does not always remember what he was saying.

At work, he is meticulous, almost rigid. He reviews patrol logs with a fine-tooth comb, looking for gaps, for patterns. His colleagues think he is dedicated; they do not know he is trying to map every possible space where a man could be taken. He avoids the section of the reserve where the incident occurred. He tells himself it is not relevant to his current duties. But when another ranger mentions that area in a meeting, Raj feels a cold wash of sweat on his back and a pressure in his chest that makes him want to stand up and leave the room. He stays, because he is a professional. He stays, and he grips the table until his knuckles are white.

He dreams of the tree. Not the men, not the ropes—just the tree. Its bark pressing into his spine. The smell of dry earth. He wakes up with his legs tangled in the sheets, heart pounding, convinced he cannot move. Anjali reaches for him, and he pushes her away without meaning to. He apologizes later. She tells him it’s okay. He doesn’t believe her.

He told me all of this in a quiet, measured voice, his eyes fixed on a point somewhere above my left shoulder. When he finished, he let his hands go still on his knees. He said, “I used to know that forest better than my own skin. Now I walk through it like a stranger. And I don’t know how to find my way back.”
